589.title: the rains
589.hook: Rama's monsoon poem: a sky that carried the sea for nine months
589.howItsDone: The monsoon is woven into Hindu poetry, music and festival life; Rama's description in the Kishkindha Kanda is often cited as an early model for the monsoon poems of later Sanskrit and Indian literature.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the rains began, a king crowned and Rama waiting in a cave. Did you do something useful while you waited? Day five hundred eighty-nine.

Some of the most famous nature writing in Sanskrit is in this chapter. Rama, waiting in the cave, describes the monsoon to Lakshmana, and it's a long, beautiful, aching poem. If you've ever been somewhere when the monsoon arrives, you'll know the feeling he's describing: the smell of wet earth after months of dust, the sky changing color in an afternoon, the whole land seeming to breathe out. Rama sees all of that, and something else too.
screen: `FAMOUS NATURE WRITING.` → `THE SMELL OF WET EARTH.` → `RAMA SEES SOMETHING ELSE TOO.`

segments.voice: Here's how Valmiki's Rama sees it. The sky, he says, drank the waters of the sea through the sun's rays, carried them for nine months, and now is giving birth to rain. That's the first image: the monsoon as a long pregnancy, finally delivered. He sees clouds piled like mountains and mountains wrapped in clouds. He hears peacocks crying out and sees them dancing. He hears frogs waking and calling after the long dry months. He watches rivers swell and rush toward the sea. And yet the rain that is lovely for everyone is painful for him. Travelers are heading home, he says. Kings have stopped their campaigns. Everyone is going back to the one they love, and he can't. So every lovely thing he sees, he sees as someone separated from Sita. In Sanskrit poetry that feeling has a name, viraha, love in separation, and Rama in the rains became one of its great examples. Poets for centuries after wrote monsoon verses in the same key: someone far from the one they love, clouds overhead, and the rain saying what they can't. The poem is doing something for Rama, too, not only for us. Describing the rain carefully slows him down. He isn't raging, and he isn't collapsing. He's looking. Lakshmana listens. And four months, one cloud at a time, begin to pass.
screen: `THE SKY CARRIED THE SEA.` · `PEACOCKS, FROGS, SWOLLEN RIVERS.` · `VIRAHA: LOVE IN SEPARATION.` · `LOOKING SLOWS HIM DOWN.`

segments.voice: Sit, and pick one thing in front of you or out the window. Describe it to yourself, slowly, the way Rama described the rain: its color, its edges, the light on it, whether it's still or moving, what it reminds you of. Breathe between each detail. Don't hurry to the next thing. If your mind drifts to something you're missing, let that be part of the looking too, and then come back. The bell holds the time.
The rains. Rama's monsoon poem: a sky carrying the sea for nine months, and every lovely thing seen through missing Sita.
Your line: the rains. Today, describe one ordinary thing you see, in a message or out loud, as carefully as you can. Day five hundred eighty-nine.

590.title: the rains
590.hook: a new king forgets, a counselor remembers, and autumn arrives
590.howItsDone: Autumn (sharad) opens the Hindu festival season, with Navaratri and Dussehra; in many places Dussehra celebrates Rama's victory, and Ramlila performances are staged in the weeks around it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the rains, and Rama's poem of the monsoon: the sky giving birth to rain. Did you describe one ordinary thing carefully? Day five hundred ninety.

Down in Kishkindha, the new king is having a wonderful time. Valmiki doesn't hide it. Sugriva has his kingdom back after years on the run. He has his wife Ruma back, and Tara is in the palace as his queen as well. He spends the season in comfort, feasting and drinking, with music in the halls. Up on the mountain, the rain falls on a cave. Then the rains end. The sky clears. And Sugriva hasn't noticed.
screen: `A WONDERFUL TIME IN KISHKINDHA.` → `MUSIC IN THE HALLS.` → `THE RAINS END, UNNOTICED.`

segments.voice: Hanuman notices. He's the one who goes to Sugriva first, before anyone gets angry. And he speaks the way he always speaks, carefully. You have your kingdom, he says. You have your glory. Now it's time to help your friends. Rama helped you; it's your turn. A king who forgets a friend's service when the time comes loses everyone's respect. Don't wait to be asked. Sugriva hears him, and orders his commanders to gather the monkey armies from every mountain and forest, within fifteen days. First idea: friendship sometimes needs a reminder, and the best reminder comes early and gently, from someone who cares about both sides. Second: the season turns. Autumn arrives, sharad, and Valmiki turns to a new kind of description. Rivers clear and slow down and show their sandbanks. The sky is clean and blue. Cranes fly. Lotuses open. Roads are passable again. It's the season kings set out. Third: for Rama, autumn is an alarm. Up on Prasravana he looks at the clear sky and knows the waiting time is over, and there's no word from Sugriva. He has been patient for four months. Now he begins to wonder whether his friend has forgotten him entirely. The rains are over. Tomorrow, Rama sends a message, and he sends it by his brother, who is not in a gentle mood.
screen: `HANUMAN REMINDS SUGRIVA.` · `ARMIES ORDERED IN FIFTEEN DAYS.` · `SHARAD: AUTUMN'S CLEAR SKY.` · `RAMA HEARS NO WORD.`

segments.voice: Sit, and bring to mind someone who did something for you that you haven't returned yet. Not to feel guilty. Just to remember. Breathe in, and see their face. Breathe out, and let one small way to repay them come to mind. Then let the plan go, and simply breathe until the bell, the way a clear autumn sky simply is. The bell holds the time.
The rains. They end in a clear autumn sky, Hanuman's early reminder, and Rama wondering whether his friend forgot.
Your line: the rains. Today, gently remind a friend of something they meant to do, or do the thing you meant to do. Day five hundred ninety.

591.title: Lakshmana's warning
591.hook: the path Vali took is not closed
591.howItsDone: Rama's message to Sugriva is one of the most quoted lines of the Kishkindha Kanda, and storytellers often use this episode to talk about keeping one's word to a friend.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the rains ended. Hanuman reminded Sugriva early and gently, and autumn came. Did you remind someone, or do the thing you'd meant to do? Day five hundred ninety-one.

Autumn sky, clear and blue. Four months of waiting, done. And no messenger from Kishkindha. Rama looks down the mountain toward the city where his friend is enjoying a throne Rama won for him. He doesn't know about Hanuman's reminder or the orders that went out. All he sees is a clear road and a silent city. His patience, which has held through grief and rain, finally gives way. Valmiki lets us hear all of it.
screen: `AUTUMN, AND NO MESSENGER.` → `A SILENT CITY BELOW.` → `PATIENCE GIVES WAY.`

segments.voice: Rama speaks to Lakshmana, first in grief, then in anger. The time we agreed on is here, he says, and Sugriva hasn't come. He's drunk on his good fortune. He thinks I'm weak, a man without a kingdom, someone he can forget. So Rama gives Lakshmana a message to carry, and it isn't subtle. Tell him: the path Vali took is not closed. Keep your word, or follow Vali. That's the first idea, and it's a hard one. A friendship sworn before fire has weight when it's broken. Rama gave first, at real cost, and he expects faith kept. Notice he doesn't ask for gratitude. He asks for the promise. Second idea: watch Lakshmana. Rama is angry. Lakshmana is angrier. He wants to go down and kill Sugriva today. So Rama, even while sending him, has to calm his brother: don't kill him. Speak gently first. Remind him of the friendship. In this pair, the one who usually does the calming has swapped places. Third: the word that matters here is samaya, an agreement, and also an appointed time. In Sanskrit it can mean both. Rama's complaint isn't that Sugriva enjoyed himself after years of exile. It's that he let the agreed time slip by. A promise has a when as well as a what. Lakshmana picks up his bow and walks down the mountain toward Kishkindha.
screen: `RAMA'S GRIEF TURNS TO ANGER.` · `THE PATH VALI TOOK IS NOT CLOSED.` · `SPEAK GENTLY FIRST.` · `SAMAYA: AGREEMENT AND TIME.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think about one promise with a date on it: a deadline, a visit, a reply you said you'd send. Breathe in, and feel where it sits in time, near or far. Breathe out, and let your body relax around it. You don't have to act on it now. Just know when it is. Promises have a when as well as a what. The bell holds the time.
Lakshmana's warning. Rama's message: the path Vali took is not closed. Keep the agreed time.
Your line: Lakshmana's warning. Today, check one promise with a date on it, and make sure you'll be on time. Day five hundred ninety-one.

592.title: Lakshmana's warning
592.hook: a bowstring that shakes a city, and the one person who can calm it
592.howItsDone: Commentators and storytellers often point to Tara here as a model of wise speech; she is one of the women the tradition remembers for her counsel as much as for her story.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lakshmana's warning set out, carrying Rama's hard message down the mountain. Did you check a promise with a date on it? Day five hundred ninety-two.
screen: `THE PATH VALI TOOK IS NOT CLOSED.`

segments.voice: The monkeys at the gates of Kishkindha see Lakshmana coming and panic. He looks, Valmiki says, like the fire at the end of the world. They scramble up walls and into trees. Some grab boulders and branches, as if that would help. Young Angada goes to meet him and is sent running back inside with the message. Lakshmana walks straight through the city, past the fine houses and gardens, and when he reaches the palace, he twangs his bowstring so loudly that the whole city shakes.
screen: `PANIC AT THE GATES.` → `LIKE THE FIRE AT THE END OF THE WORLD.` → `A BOWSTRING SHAKES THE CITY.`

segments.voice: Inside, Sugriva hears the bowstring, and the party is over. He's frightened, and he knows he's in the wrong. But it's his fear that decides who goes out to meet Lakshmana. He sends Tara. First idea: of everyone in the palace, Tara is the one who can calm this. Not long ago she was a widow grieving before Rama. Now she walks out to meet his furious brother, and she speaks with complete poise. Why are you angry, prince? she asks. Sugriva has been careless, yes. After years of hardship he's been lost in pleasure. Even great sages have been carried away by desire, she says, and she names Vishvamitra, who once spent years with the celestial dancer Ghritachi and thought it was a single day. Second idea: she tells him the part he hasn't heard. Sugriva hasn't actually forgotten. Orders have already gone out. Armies are already on their way, from mountains and forests everywhere. Come in, she says. Talk to him. Third: watch what her words do. Lakshmana came in furious. He listens, and his anger cools. He doesn't stop being firm, but now he's willing to talk. It's one of the quiet surprises of the Kishkindha Kanda: the person who turns aside Rama's warning is the same person whose own warning Vali ignored. Tara has been right twice now. This time somebody listens.
screen: `SUGRIVA SENDS TARA.` · `EVEN SAGES ARE CARRIED AWAY.` · `THE ARMIES ARE ALREADY COMING.` · `THIS TIME SOMEBODY LISTENS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and recall a time someone was angry with you, and fairly. Breathe in, and remember how it felt in your body. Now imagine meeting that anger the way Tara did: calm, honest, admitting the part that's true, explaining the part that isn't. Breathe out. You don't need to rehearse the words. Just let your body learn what calm in front of anger might feel like. The bell holds the time.
Lakshmana's warning. Delivered with a bowstring, and met by Tara: yes, he was careless, and the armies are already coming.
Your line: Lakshmana's warning. Today, if someone's upset with you, admit the true part first, then explain the rest. Day five hundred ninety-two.

593.title: Lakshmana's warning
593.hook: an apology, a flood of armies, and an embrace
593.howItsDone: Kshama, forgiveness or forbearance, is listed among the virtues in many Hindu texts, and the Ramayana's reconciliation of Rama and Sugriva is often told as an example of friendship repaired.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lakshmana's warning met Tara's calm, and the anger cooled. Did you admit the true part first? Day five hundred ninety-three.

Lakshmana walks into the inner palace. It's beautiful, full of gardens, music and fine things, and Valmiki describes it in detail, maybe so we'll feel how far Sugriva has drifted from a cave on a mountain. Sugriva is on his throne, dressed in fine clothes and garlands, his queens around him. He sees Lakshmana and gets to his feet. Now the king of the monkeys has to face the brother of the man who made him king.
screen: `THE INNER PALACE.` → `SUGRIVA ON HIS THRONE.` → `HE GETS TO HIS FEET.`

segments.voice: Lakshmana speaks hard words. A king who takes help and doesn't keep his promise is ungrateful, he says, and for ingratitude there's no atonement. He repeats Rama's message. Sugriva doesn't argue. And here Valmiki gives him one of his best moments. Everything I have, he says, I owe to Rama. I may have slipped. Who doesn't? But I'm his friend and his servant, and I'll follow him with my whole army. If I've failed through carelessness or overconfidence, forgive me. First idea: a good apology owns the fault, doesn't drown in it, and moves to action. Sugriva does all three. Lakshmana softens at once. You've spoken well, he says. Come and see Rama. Second idea: the armies arrive. Valmiki turns it into a parade. Monkeys and bears pour in by the thousand, from mountains and seashores, from forests and snowy peaks, until they seem to cover the earth. Sugriva rides out with Lakshmana to Rama, gets down, and bows with joined palms. Third: Rama receives him with an embrace. No lecture. He asks him to sit beside him. The Sanskrit word for forgiveness, kshama, also means patience, and it's also a name for the earth, the one who bears everything. Rama doesn't hold on to the late autumn. The friendship is back where it was, and stronger, because now it has been tested and repaired. And Rama turns to the real question: where do we look first?
screen: `NO ATONEMENT FOR INGRATITUDE.` · `SUGRIVA: FORGIVE ME.` · `ARMIES COVER THE EARTH.` · `KSHAMA: FORGIVENESS, THE EARTH.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of a small fault of yours that someone might still be holding. Breathe in, and own it privately and plainly: yes, I did that. Breathe out, and let yourself also be someone who can be forgiven. Then think of someone you could forgive, and let your hand open on your knee, palm up, for the rest of the sit. The bell holds the time.
Lakshmana's warning. It ends in Sugriva's apology, a flood of armies, and Rama's embrace.

594.title: the search parties
594.hook: four armies, four directions, and a map learned by running
594.howItsDone: Sugriva's descriptions of the four directions are studied as an early Indian picture of the world; many places named in them, from the Ganga to the southern sea, are still pilgrimage sites linked to the Ramayana.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lakshmana's warning ended in an apology and an embrace, and armies covering the earth. Did you own one small fault? Day five hundred ninety-four.

The rains are over and the roads are open. Sugriva stands before an army gathered from every forest and mountain he rules, and he has almost nothing to hand it: a bundle of jewels, a name, and one direction. The chariot flew south. That's all anyone knows. Somewhere beyond the forests and rivers and seas is one woman, and no one has an address. Sugriva's answer is to split the army four ways, and to give each leader directions so detailed they fill whole chapters.
screen: `ONE WOMAN, SOMEWHERE.` → `A HUGE ARMY, NO ADDRESS.` → `SPLIT FOUR WAYS.`

segments.voice: Sugriva sends Vinata to the east, Sushena to the west, Shatabali to the north, and to the south, where Ravana flew, he sends his best: Angada, with Hanuman, the old bear Jambavan, and others. Start with the lists. Sugriva doesn't just say go east. For each direction he names rivers, mountains, kingdoms and peoples, seas and islands, and strange places at the edge of the world. Scholars sometimes call these chapters the epic's geography: a picture of the world as the poem imagined it. Some names match real places, like the Ganga, the Yamuna and the Godavari. Others belong to myth, like the mountains where the sun rises and sets. Then there's the question of how Sugriva knows all this. Rama asks him later: how do you know the whole earth so well? Sugriva answers that when Vali was chasing him, he fled everywhere, and saw the whole world while running for his life. His exile became his map. The worst years of his life turn out to be exactly what his friend needs. And there's a deadline. One month, Sugriva says. Come back within a month, with news, or answer to me with your lives. It's harsh. But it shows how seriously he now takes the promise he once let slip. The armies set out in four directions, and the city goes quiet behind them. Rama, Lakshmana and Sugriva stay behind, which may be the hardest job of all: waiting a month for news.
screen: `EAST, WEST, NORTH, AND SOUTH.` · `THE EPIC'S GEOGRAPHY.` · `A MAP LEARNED BY RUNNING.` · `ONE MONTH.`

segments.voice: Sit, and feel the four directions around you: in front, behind, left, right. Breathe in, and sense the space ahead. Breathe out, and sense the space behind. Then the left, and then the right. Let yourself sit in the middle of all four, centered and still. For these two minutes, there's nowhere to go. The bell holds the time.
The search parties. Four armies, four directions, a map Sugriva learned by running, and one month.
Your line: the search parties. Today, break one big task into four parts, and start the first one. Day five hundred ninety-four.

595.title: the search parties
595.hook: a ring with Rama's name, and three parties come home empty-handed
595.howItsDone: Rama's ring is one of the best-known objects in the Ramayana; in art Hanuman is often shown kneeling before Sita and offering it, and the scene is a favorite in temple carvings and paintings.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the search parties, four armies, four directions, one month. Did you break a big task into parts? Today the week closes. Day five hundred ninety-five.

Before the southern party leaves, Rama calls Hanuman aside. Of all the leaders and all the armies, it's Hanuman he picks out. Sugriva's confidence in him is obvious. And Rama has his own reasons, going back to that first conversation on Rishyamuka, the sentence with not one word wrong. He takes something small off his finger and holds it out. It's the kind of thing you'd give someone only if you were sure of them.
screen: `RAMA CALLS HANUMAN ASIDE.` → `SOMETHING SMALL, HELD OUT.`

segments.voice: It's a ring, engraved with Rama's name. Take this, Rama tells him, so that when you find her, she'll know you come from me, and won't be afraid. First idea: a token. Hanuman will meet Sita as a stranger, a monkey in an enemy city. Words alone might not be believed. A ring she knows will be. Rama is planning ahead for the moment when trust will matter most. Second idea: why Hanuman. Valmiki says it plainly. Sugriva is surest of him, and Rama sees his determination and believes this one will succeed. A ring given to one messenger is a lot of hope in one small object. And Hanuman takes it, Valmiki says, with joined palms, bowing, as if he'd been handed something holy. Third: the month passes. The parties to the east, the west and the north search everything Sugriva described: mountains, forests, caves, rivers, cities. They come back on time, and they come back with nothing. No sign of Sita, they tell Sugriva. Now everyone is waiting on the south. Now the week, from the top. The monsoon poem, the sky giving birth to rain. Hanuman's early reminder, and a clear autumn sky. Rama's message: the path Vali took is not closed. Lakshmana's bowstring, and Tara's calm. Sugriva's apology, and armies covering the earth. Four directions and a map learned by running. And today, a ring, and three empty-handed returns.
screen: `A RING WITH RAMA'S NAME.` · `WHY HANUMAN.` · `THREE PARTIES RETURN EMPTY.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `EVERYONE WAITS ON THE SOUTH.`

segments.voice: If you're wearing a ring or something small you value, rest your attention on it. If not, picture something small that someone once gave you. Breathe in, and remember who gave it. Breathe out, and feel what it carries: their trust, their memory, their hope. Let that small object be your anchor for these two minutes. The bell holds the time.
The search parties. Three come home empty-handed, and the south carries Rama's ring, engraved with his name.
Your line: the search parties. Today, give someone a small token of trust: a key, a task, a word of confidence. Day five hundred ninety-five.

east, west and north all return with no news.

fork.setup: you're Rama. a stranger will have to win Sita's trust in an enemy city. what do you give him?
options: a letter.
your ring, engraved with your name.
nothing: his words will be enough.
fork.reveal: Rama gives Hanuman his ring, so Sita will know the messenger comes from him.

original.note: Sanskrit aṅgulīya: a finger-ring, from aṅguli, finger.

trapdoor: what you thought: the ring is a keepsake.
what it means: it's a token planned for the moment of trust.
what a scholar hears: Kishkindha 44 has Rama give Hanuman the ring inscribed with his name; Kishkindha 47 reports the return of the other three parties.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda 44 (Rama gives Hanuman the ring)
Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda 47 (east, west and north return)
